fullText:
Great work on harness self-improvement from Microsoft and colleagues.

It discusses how to build long-running agents that improve their own harness,

It turns out that if you run agents for hours, giving them a way to fix their own harness during the run improves results on long-running problems.

More from the paper:

Harness optimization usually runs offline.

You tune the harness on tasks that have reference answers, then reuse it. Long open-ended tasks have no reference answers, and they run into problems the tuned harness never saw.

BOXBOX moves that loop into the task itself.

The agent decides when to revise its harness, and a kernel hot-reloads the new version while keeping the full execution context, so the run continues without a restart.

They test it on PerfRace, a new benchmark where agents spend hours speeding up real software projects. Under the same time and cost budget, BOXBOX reaches a 1.70x speedup at four hours, against 1.54x for the best baseline.

https://t.co/UQgvVqgSQQ

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/9NGxXIpJ8f

fullText:
How soon should we see AI's impact in productivity statistics? 

With the PC, it took 14 years for aggregate productivity growth to show up. Economists didn't see it in their analysis for another five years. 

But work by @erikbryn and others showed individual firms seeing results by 1987 (although that work was published 9 years later.)

With genAI, individual companies will report results well before we can see aggregate impact. And our data (and others) show that some firms are reporting exactly those early results.

It shouldn't surprise people if today, four years after ChatGPT and three years after general availability of enterprise GenAI services from Microsoft and Google, we can't be confident that the strong productivity growth numbers released are really driven by GenAI. It's just too soon for big companies to show huge results and too soon for AI-native startups to be big enough to matter. 

If AI is more like electricity than the PC, and requires wholesale redesign of business operations, it might take even longer to show up in aggregate statistics.

But this doesn't mean the corporate spending on AI won't increase as firms figure out how to get better results. 

These firms will face their own individual J-curves, where their total investment runs ahead of results, even as they become successful. (The reason is that once you figure out how to succeed in one domain, you'll apply that playbook to several others, all of which will need investment before payback). 

If AI is really boosting productivity, I reckon aggregate numbers might start to persuasively (but not unimpeachably) show that by 2028.

i forgot about this until @ScottWu46 reminded me, but back in january 2017 when we were 19, scott and i had lunch in SF

at lunch, we talked about how our IMO/IOI/math competition gang could be the next paypal mafia. i knew the competition kids were geniuses by any standard, and felt confident in time we could take the tech world by storm

fast forward nearly 10 years later, and many of our friends from that time are some of the most exciting people in AI and technology (@ScottWu46, @akshat_b, @chameleon_jeff, Jerry Ma, @randomjohnnyh, @0xShitTrader, @stevenkplus1, @thejessezhang, @vickie_ye_, @alexwei_, @demi_guo_, @d_m_ziegler, @hughbzhang, @_mohansolo, @MarkSellke, and many others i'm sure i'm forgetting)

i'm now at that age where i reminisce about everyone i grew up with, and i've known most of these people since middle school (via MATHCOUNTS!). even though we were scattered around the country, we would gchat about math problems and hang out on AoPS, then we did math/algo camps together, and then we did internships together.

very crazy to think about the degree of sheer brilliance of this group when we were just teenagers, and so special to see so many go on to leave their mark on the world.

note to parents: if your kid is on gchat all day solving math problems with some anonymous group of cross-country asian kids, (s)he may just turn out alright.

fullText:
The history of weights and measures should be taught in schools!

Start here: https://t.co/eJEN7SHr3G

See this incredible piece of that history, which I found on FB/Meta:

“The US standard railroad gauge (distance between the rails) is 4 feet, 8.5 inches. That's an exceedingly odd number. Why was that gauge used?

Well, because that's the way they built them in England, and English engineers designed the first US railroads. Why did the English build them like that?

Because the first rail lines were built by the same people who built the wagon tramways, and that's the gauge they used. So, why did 'they' use that gauge then?

Because the people who built the tramways used the same jigs and tools that they had used for building wagons, which used that same wheel spacing. Why did the wagons have that particular odd wheel spacing?

Well, if they tried to use any other spacing, the wagon wheels would break more often on some of the old, long distance roads in England. You see, that's the spacing of the wheel ruts. So who built those old rutted roads?

Imperial Rome built the first long distance roads in Europe (including England) for their legions. Those roads have been used ever since. And what about the ruts in the roads?

Roman war chariots formed the initial ruts, which everyone else had to match or run the risk of destroying their wagon wheels. Since the chariots were made for Imperial Rome, they were all alike in the matter of wheel spacing. Therefore, the United States standard railroad gauge of 4 feet, 8.5 inches is derived from the original specifications for an Imperial Roman war chariot. Bureaucracies live forever.

So the next time you are handed a specification/procedure/process and wonder 'What horse's ass came up with this?', you may be exactly right. Imperial Roman army chariots were made just wide enough to accommodate the rear ends of two war horses. (Two horses' asses.)

Now, the twist to the story:

When you see a Space Shuttle sitting on its launch pad, there are two big booster rockets attached to the sides of the main fuel tank. These are solid rocket boosters, or SRBs. The SRBs are made by Thiokol at their factory in Utah. The engineers who designed the SRBs would have preferred to make them a bit fatter, but the SRBs had to be shipped by train from the factory to the launch site. The railroad line from the factory happens to run through a tunnel in the mountains, and the SRBs had to fit through that tunnel. The tunnel is slightly wider than the railroad track, and the railroad track, as you now know, is about as wide as two horses' behinds.

So, a major Space Shuttle design feature, of what is arguably the world's most advanced transportation system, was determined over two thousand years ago by the width of a horse's ass. And you thought being a horse's ass wasn't important? Ancient horse's asses control almost everything.”

fullText:
I've seen many make this mistake over and over again. 

Overrelying on someone else's harness. 

As you go deeper with agents, you quickly realize how standard, out-of-the-box harnesses constrain LLMs. 

Imo, agent harnesses need customization to unlock real gains and efficiencies.

This is why more full-stack AI companies are building harnesses in-house. You move faster when you don't wait for someone else to build the thing that keeps your agents working effectively. 

If you are locked in with a specific proprietary harness, good luck. 

If you are using an open-source agent harness, you are in better shape. You can customize it to suit your needs. 

But even then, you are relying on a harness someone else built. 

My hot take is that you want to fully own the harness. As in building it, understanding it, and maintaining it. 

The good news is that harnesses can stay minimal now, since LLMs have gotten much better at many of the things harnesses were built for (tool calling, progressive disclosure, persistence, etc.).

These days, I spend more time customizing my harness to better coordinate with my agent teams, test different memory systems, proactive patterns, and develop strategies to give it the right context. 

I can do this freely and unlock new experiences because I don't rely on anyone's harness. I think all of this is much harder to do if you are using someone else's harness. The reason is that the customization goes really deep.

fullText:
A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.
